title: Flat adverbs: the same form as the adjective
lede: Adverbs with no *-ly* — *fast*, *hard*, *late*, *straight* — that look like adjectives and are not mistakes.
intro: A flat adverb has the same form as its adjective. These are the older English adverbs that survived the spread of *-ly*, and they are fully standard: *drive fast*, *work hard*, *arrive late*. The trap is the reverse assumption — that adding *-ly* always gives the same meaning. For many of these words it gives a different word entirely, and that partner is in group 3. American speech also uses many informal flat adverbs (*drive slow*, *come quick*, *hold tight*) that formal writing avoids; each entry says which kind it is.

title: Adverbs with irregular comparison
lede: The handful of adverbs that do not take *-er* or *more*: *well*, *badly*, *much*, *little*, *far* and their forms.
intro: Almost every gradable adverb compares with *-er/-est* (*faster*) or *more/most* (*more carefully*). A few do neither and have forms that must simply be learned — *well*, *better*, *best*; *badly*, *worse*, *worst*. Each comparative and superlative has its own entry, because *better* and *further* do work of their own (*you had better go*, *discuss it further*) that the base word never does.

title: The -ly form that means something else
lede: *hardly*, *lately*, *nearly*, *highly* — the *-ly* forms whose meaning drifted away from the flat adverb they look like.
intro: Adding *-ly* to *hard* does not give a more formal way of saying *with effort* — it gives *hardly*, which means *almost not*. The same drift happened to *late*/*lately*, *near*/*nearly*, *high*/*highly* and a dozen more. These are among the most frequent errors in learner English, because the spelling promises a relationship the meaning no longer has. Every entry names its flat partner and says exactly how they differ.

title: Adverbs of place
lede: Where? — *here*, *there*, *everywhere*, *upstairs*, *abroad*, *home*, and the words that locate without an object.
intro: Place adverbs answer *where?* and normally go at the end of the clause. Many of them look like prepositions (*inside*, *above*, *behind*) and become adverbs simply by dropping the object: *wait inside the car* is a preposition, *wait inside* is an adverb. The one that catches Russian speakers is *home*, which takes no preposition after verbs of motion — *go home*, never *go to home*.

title: Adverbs of direction and adverbial particles
lede: Where to? — *up*, *down*, *back*, *forward*, *sideways*, *clockwise*, and the particles that complete phrasal verbs.
intro: Direction adverbs answer *where to?* or *which way?*. A large part of this group doubles as the particles of phrasal verbs — *turn **off***, *give **up***, *come **back*** — which is where their meaning stops being about direction at all. Each entry lists the literal directional sense first and then the most important non-literal ones; the phrasal verbs themselves are in the verb dictionary.

title: Adverbs of time
lede: When? — *now*, *soon*, *already*, *yet*, *still*, *recently*, *ago*, and the words that place an event on the timeline.
intro: Time adverbs locate an event relative to now or to another event. Several of them are tied to a tense: *already*, *yet* and *just* pull toward the present perfect in American and British English alike, although American speech also allows the simple past (*Did you eat yet?*). *Ago* is the odd one out — it follows its time phrase (*three days ago*) and cannot be used with the present perfect.

title: Adverbs of frequency and duration
intro: Indefinite frequency adverbs sit on a scale from *always* to *never* and take mid-position: after *be*, before the main verb, after the first auxiliary. Definite frequency adverbs (*daily*, *weekly*, *twice*) go at the end instead. Duration adverbs answer *how long?*. Getting the position right matters more here than anywhere else in the dictionary, because *I go always* is the error every teacher hears.

title: Degree adverbs that turn it up
lede: How much? — *very*, *really*, *so*, *too*, *quite*, *extremely*, *totally*, *absolutely* and the other intensifiers.
intro: Intensifiers strengthen an adjective, an adverb or a verb. The key distinction is gradable versus extreme: *very* goes with gradable adjectives (*very cold*) and *absolutely* with extreme ones (*absolutely freezing*), and mixing them (*very freezing*, *absolutely cold*) sounds wrong to a native ear. *Too* means *more than is wanted*, not *very* — *too expensive* is a complaint. And *quite* means *very* in American English but often only *fairly* in British English.

title: Degree adverbs that turn it down
intro: Downtoners weaken or approximate. Several carry negative force (*barely*, *scarcely*) and so cannot be combined with another negative. *Almost* and *nearly* are close but not identical, *enough* follows an adjective instead of preceding it (*old enough*, not *enough old*), and *kind of* and *sort of* are the everyday American hedges that formal writing replaces with *somewhat*.

title: Focusing adverbs
intro: A focusing adverb points at one part of the sentence and either restricts attention to it (*only*, *merely*, *especially*) or adds it to something already said (*also*, *too*, *even*). Moving one changes the meaning — *Only Ana saw it* and *Ana only saw it* say different things — so every entry here gives its position rule with a pair of examples. *Either* replaces *too* in negative sentences: *I don’t like it either*.

title: Stance and comment adverbs
lede: What the speaker thinks of it — *probably*, *maybe*, *obviously*, *luckily*, *frankly*, *actually*, *of course*.
intro: Stance adverbs comment on the whole statement rather than on the verb: how certain it is (*probably*, *definitely*), how the speaker feels about it (*unfortunately*, *luckily*), or how it is being said (*frankly*, *honestly*). Most go at the front with a comma or in mid-position. Two are false friends for Russian speakers — *actually* means *in fact*, not *актуально*, and *eventually* means *in the end*, not *возможно*.

title: Viewpoint and domain adverbs
lede: From this point of view — *financially*, *technically*, *legally*, *personally*, *ideally*, *strictly speaking*.
intro: Viewpoint adverbs narrow the frame in which a statement is true: *Financially, it makes sense* claims nothing about whether it makes sense in any other way. They usually open the sentence with a comma. The pattern is productive — almost any *-al* adjective can do it — so this group lists the frequent ones and the ones whose viewpoint sense differs from their manner sense (*technically*, *practically*, *personally*).

title: Linking adverbs
lede: How this sentence relates to the last one — *however*, *therefore*, *moreover*, *instead*, *otherwise*, *anyway*.
intro: Linking (conjunctive) adverbs connect a sentence to the one before it, but grammatically they are adverbs, not conjunctions — which is why *It rained, however we went* is a punctuation error: two sentences joined only by a comma. Use a period or a semicolon before them. The conjunction dictionary covers them as connectors; these entries cover them as adverbs, with the positions they can take inside a clause.

title: Question and relative adverbs
lede: *when*, *where*, *why*, *how* — asking about circumstances, and introducing clauses about time, place and reason.
intro: The same four words ask questions (*Where did you park?*) and introduce relative clauses (*the lot where I parked*). In indirect questions the word order returns to normal — *Do you know where I parked?*, not *where did I park* — which is the most persistent error with this group. The *-ever* compounds (*wherever*, *whenever*, *however*) mean *no matter where/when/how*.

title: Negative and function adverbs
lede: *not*, *no*, *any*, *as*, *else*, *together* — the small grammatical adverbs that everything else leans on.
intro: *Not* is an adverb, and the most frequent one in the language. With it here are the function adverbs that do grammatical work rather than adding meaning: *no* and *any* before a comparative (*no better*, *any faster*), *as* in comparisons of equality (*as tall as*), *else* after a question word or indefinite (*who else*, *something else*), and *together* and *all* in their adverb uses (*all alone*).
